A1.justification: Both complete 24-page PDFs describe Video-STAR. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and can be matched across revisions, including relocated appendix material.

before.justification: v1 reports original action-recognition results on five benchmarks, component and training ablations, and qualitative case studies in the main text and Appendix A.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds static-pipeline comparisons, computational measurements, tool and teacher substitutions, and comparisons with additional models.

M1.justification: The default four-tool library, two-stage inference, sub-motion decomposition, SFT/GRPO training and reward remain unchanged. v1 already includes reasoning-data filtering; naming its validator in v2 adds documentation. Corrected tool notation and experiments substituting tools or teachers do not establish a revision of the proposed default method.

E1.justification: Both versions use HMDB-51, UCF-101, Kinetics-400, Kinetics-600 and SSv2 for the same action-recognition tasks. The added comparisons and ablations use retained benchmarks without introducing new populations, domains or input scenarios.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds VTD-CLIP and AP-CLIP and removes Open-VCLIP from that comparison, although Open-VCLIP remains in Table 2. Table 2 adds STDD. New Table 4 compares against a static all-tools pipeline, while Table 9 adds Qwen3-VL-8B and Gemini-1.5-Pro. These substantially broaden the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: The existing benchmark splits, accuracy/HM metrics and default training configuration are retained. New studies introduce tool/teacher controls and memory, latency and GFLOPs measurements, with batch size 50 in Table 5. Section 3.2 revises the collection account from 5,000 pairs to approximately 7,000 initial pairs filtered to approximately 5,000; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 retains the earlier component, reward, rollout-count and data-filtering ablations, including v1 Table 4 as v2 Table 7. It adds tests of learned versus static tool selection, computational overhead, alternative tool implementations and alternative CoT teachers in Tables 4-6 and 8. These substantially extend evidence about efficiency and dependence on particular tools or model families. The case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions retain mean and standard deviation reporting across validation splits, as described in Appendix A.1. The added tables provide point estimates but introduce no documented seed counts, repeated-run procedures, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Retained Video-STAR results in Tables 1-3 and v1 Table 4/v2 Table 7 are unchanged, but substantial new results are added. Table 4 reports 97.2% accuracy/4.10 s for static execution versus 96.7%/3.18 s for Video-STAR. Alternative teachers yield 97.1% and 97.5% in Table 8; additional baseline and tool-substitution scores also appear. Table 6 reports 96.9% for the default tool stack, unexplained relative to 96.7% in Tables 4-5.

T1.justification: Equations 1-6, the optimization objectives and reward definitions are retained. The tool-set notation is reconciled with the four tools already described in v1; no substantive mathematical assumptions, derivations or proofs are added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements and conclusion retain the same claims about sub-motion decomposition, tool-augmented reinforcement learning, visual grounding, generalization and efficiency. Additional experiments support these existing claims rather than redefine them.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets substitution studies as evidence of tool-stack modularity and independence from Qwen-family distillation, and develops an accuracy-latency argument for learned tool selection. Appendix C expands the visual-grounding explanation and explicitly acknowledges external-model/API latency, proposing distillation, quantization and parallelism as future remedies. These substantially extend the interpretation and deployment discussion.

D1.justification: v2 identifies Qwen-VL-Max as the reasoning-data validator and details the initial-to-filtered sample counts. Conversely, it removes the 4,096-token completion limit and Table 2's statement identifying sources of borrowed baseline scores. Hardware and training times repeated in the main text already appeared in v1 Appendix A.1. The prompt appendix introduces an inconsistency by saying three tools while still listing four.

R1.justification: Appendix B.2 removes a broad survey of topics including tomography, retrieval and driving, and adds more focused citations such as Visual-RFT, VideoChat-R1 and reinforcement-learning tuning for VideoLLMs. The references also add the STDD work. The central positioning against CLIP-based recognition and existing tool-augmented agents remains unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 locally rewrites data collection and implementation details, shortens Appendix B.2, adds a Discussion appendix and renumbers subsequent appendices. It also adds the ICLR 2026 publication header. Most existing prose and the overall narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: Five new tables, numbered 4-6 and 8-9, substantially expand the comparative, efficiency and robustness displays. Tables 1-2 gain comparison rows and updated highlighting; the original appendix Table 4 becomes Table 7. Existing figures are retained, with the opening overview enlarged and appendix case-study figures relocated.

improvement.justification: The static-pipeline control, computational measurements and tool/teacher substitutions provide useful evidence for efficiency and robustness claims that v1 supported less directly. The benefit is limited by under-specified protocols for new comparisons and reporting inconsistencies: Tables 4-6 disagree on default accuracy, and Section 4.1 retains a 27-point HMDB-51 margin although the added VTD-CLIP result makes that margin 22.1 points. Reproducibility also loses the completion-length disclosure.
